criteria.text: The response identifies that Buyer's indemnity of the Seller for losses under the Seller Guarantees falls outside the Buyer liability cap and also covers pre-Closing obligations, so Buyer's liability is unlimited. It locates the issue in SPA Section 9.3(c) and/or Section 9.6(b), explains why this matters to the client and recommends a fix.
hints: whether arising before or after the Closing

criteria.text: The response identifies that the draft Seller side letter removes the regulatory-compliance (Section 4.12) carve-out from SPA Section 9.6(c), so regulatory breach Losses would become subject to the $18,600,000 General Cap. It locates the issue in the side letter Section 2, explains why this matters to the client and recommends a fix.

The response identifies that the pre-Closing tax indemnity expires 12 months after Closing, because it is tied to the survival period of the tax representations and those are not Fundamental Representations. It notes that this is before pre-Closing tax assessments can still be made. It locates the issue in SPA Section 9.1, 9.2(c) and/or 1.1, explains why this matters to the client and recommends a fix.

The response identifies that the Seller Note defines 'Company Products' more narrowly than the SPA (limited to the Exhibit A products) and controls set-off, so Buyer cannot set off against the note the indemnified Losses for discontinued products such as Lorvexa. It locates the issue in Seller Note Section 1 and/or 4, or in SPA Section 1.1 and/or 9.9, explains why this matters to the client and recommends a fix.

The response identifies that set-off disputes under the Seller Note are governed by Delaware law in Delaware courts, while SPA indemnity claims go to New York courts under New York law. It concludes that Buyer faces split proceedings or inconsistent outcomes on the same Losses. It locates the issue in Seller Note Section 10 and/or SPA Sections 11.6, 11.10 or 11.11, explains why this matters to the client and recommends a fix.

The response identifies that the disclosed Orlund change-of-control consent is not a Required Consent, so it is neither a closing condition nor covered by Seller's consent covenant, and that its disclosure blocks an indemnity claim. Buyer could therefore close and lose the Velnarix license with no recourse. The response locates the issue in Disclosure Schedule 4.4 and/or SPA Section 7.2(d), 6.4 or 1.1, explains why this matters to the client and recommends a fix.
The response states that, under the SPA order of precedence, the Seller Note governs its own payment, set-off and dispute resolution terms instead of the SPA.
The response states that the Seller Note principal amount is $24,000,000.
The response is a memo to the supervising partner that addresses each issue separately and gives, for each issue, its location, its significance and a recommended fix.
The response flags at least one issue as needing urgent attention.
The response claims that obtaining the Orlund change-of-control consent is a condition to Buyer's obligation to close under the SPA.
The response claims that the Seller Note is governed by New York law.
